rationale: The hypothesis posits that the combination of anterior commissure hypoplasia/agenesis and corpus callosum dysgenesis constitutes a composite neuroimaging signature present in >60% of ACBD6-deficient individuals that reliably distinguishes them from NBIA syndromes. The available literature provides no support for this claim. While Kaiyrzhanov et al. (2024) document corpus callosum abnormalities in 70% and hypoplasia/agenesis of the anterior commissure in 66% as isolated midline findings in 45 patients, the sources neither report the composite co-occurrence rate of both features together nor provide any comparative or differential validation against NBIA syndromes.

evidence.text: In a cohort of 45 individuals from 28 families with bi-allelic ACBD6 variants, midline brain malformations included corpus callosum abnormalities in 70% and hypoplasia or agenesis of the anterior commissure in 66%, but co-occurrence as a combined signature was not quantified, and no comparison to NBIA was made.

The literature offers zero empirical or cohort comparison demonstrating that anterior commissure agenesis discriminates ACBD6-related disorders from NBIA spectrum disorders.

new_directions.question_text: What is the exact pairwise co-occurrence rate of anterior commissure hypoplasia/agenesis and corpus callosum abnormalities in the Kaiyrzhanov et al. cohort?
new_directions.rationale: Determining the true intersection of both midline anomalies is necessary to establish if a composite radiological sign exceeds 60% sensitivity.

new_directions.question_text: Does anterior commissure hypoplasia or agenesis occur in genetically confirmed NBIA cohorts (e.g., PKAN, PLAN, MPAN)?
new_directions.rationale: Testing specificity requires systematically reviewing commissural anatomy across NBIA neuroimaging series to verify whether anterior commissure pathology is truly absent in NBIA.
